lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand the role of diffusion in gas exchange
understand gas exchange (of carbon dioxide and oxygen) in relation to respiration and photosynthesis

primer.text: Diffusion is the engine of every gas exchange, from an amoeba's membrane to a leaf's stomata. This note starts with the rule itself, then applies it to the plant: which gas crosses where, and how photosynthesis and respiration each set the direction.

modules.title: Diffusion and Exchange Surfaces
modules.opening: Particles wander constantly, and diffusion is the net result: movement from where a substance is more concentrated to where it is less so, down the gradient. Single-celled organisms like amoeba manage on their membranes alone; bigger organisms need exchange surfaces — gills, lungs, leaves — built large, thin and, in animals, well ventilated.
keyPoints: Diffusion moves particles from higher to lower concentration, down a gradient.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the molecules that move this way in gas exchange.
Amoeba exchanges gases straight through its cell membrane.
Multicellular organisms use dedicated exchange surfaces and organ systems.
Effective surfaces share a large area, a thin barrier and steep gradients.

low.restatement: Diffusion is downhill travel for particles, and exchange surfaces make the hill short and wide.
low.analogy: A stadium exit: many wide gates (area) set close to the car park (short distance) empty fastest.
low.examPointer: Quote the three surface features — large, thin, gradient-keeping — for the full mechanism.

medium.restatement: Large, thin and refreshed — the three laws of any exchange surface.
medium.analogy: A motorway works when it has many lanes, short bridges and steady traffic flow.
medium.examPointer: When comparing organisms, always tie a surface feature to faster exchange.

modules.title: Gas Exchange in Respiration
modules.opening: Respiration never pauses, so a plant always consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. At night, with photosynthesis switched off, that consumption is all there is: oxygen diffuses into the leaf down its gradient and carbon dioxide diffuses out, each crossing wherever the leaf lets it.
keyPoints: All living cells respire day and night, consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide.
At night no photosynthesis runs, so respiration alone sets the exchange.
Oxygen diffuses into the leaf from the higher concentration outside.
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the leaf to the lower concentration outside.
Respiring cells keep their internal oxygen low, which maintains the inward gradient.

low.restatement: At night the leaf behaves like any animal tissue: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out.
low.analogy: A shop that only receives deliveries (oxygen) and puts out rubbish (carbon dioxide) after dark.
low.examPointer: Name both directions in your answer — inward oxygen and outward carbon dioxide.

medium.restatement: Respiring cells set the gradients that drive both gas movements.
medium.analogy: A furnace that consumes wood and emits smoke: the difference from the surroundings keeps both flows going.
medium.examPointer: Write the words concentration gradient next to each gas for the mechanism marks.

modules.title: Gas Exchange in Photosynthesis
modules.opening: In daylight the leaf's chemistry flips. Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide, so the inside stays low and the gas is drawn in from the air; oxygen, made as a product, piles up and diffuses out. The gradients are the same tools, pointed the other way.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
Cells using chloroplasts keep internal carbon dioxide low while photosynthesising.
Carbon dioxide therefore diffuses from outside the leaf inwards.
Oxygen produced inside diffuses outwards, down its own gradient.
Some of the released oxygen is immediately spent by respiration.

low.restatement: Photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide in and pushes oxygen out.
low.analogy: A kitchen cooking with the window open: ingredients come in, steam goes out, both following their own gradients.
low.examPointer: State the direction for both gases and note that respiration still runs underneath.

medium.restatement: The faster process owns the net flow; the slower one trims it.
medium.analogy: Two taps filling and draining one basin: the stronger tap decides whether the level rises or falls.
medium.examPointer: Use the word net when comparing photosynthesis and respiration — examiners look for it.

glossary.definition: The difference in a substance's level between two regions; diffusion runs down it.
A body surface over which substances enter and leave; large, thin and gradient-keeping when effective.
The overall direction of gas movement after the faster of photosynthesis and respiration has set the balance.
